paras: The threatened lynching of Jacob Whitmore occurred at Bellefontaine, Ohio, in early October 1881, when crowds gathered to hang Whitmore, a young farmer jailed on the charge of poisoning his wife. Sheriff H. M. Cline took him to a neighboring county before the crowd could act, and militia guarded the jail through the night. Whitmore was later indicted for first-degree murder; no paper gives the race of anyone involved.

Whitmore, a farmer given as about 28, had married Orrie Short, daughter of Reuben Short, on July 17; the papers gave her age as 14 or 16. On the afternoon of Friday, September 30, the couple went into the woods near their home at Huntsville, eight or nine miles from Bellefontaine, to gather hickory nuts with two young children of her family. She came home with cramps and spasms and died about midnight, after saying that her husband had made her swallow a white powder, threatening her with a knife.

Whitmore was arrested and said that his wife had taken the poison voluntarily. At the inquest on Saturday, witnesses testified that he had bought strychnine two weeks earlier, and her little brother confirmed her statement. The preliminary examination was reported to give 'almost positive proof of the prisoner's guilt.'

The Times correspondent at Bellefontaine had predicted that Whitmore 'may be lynched' if the evidence was strong, recalling an earlier lynching there in 'the notorious Shell case.' According to a German-language dispatch dated October 4, Sheriff Cline received word that a mob intended to come and lynch Whitmore, put him in a wagon, and drove him to the neighboring county. The same report said the sheriff also feared the town would lynch Hoge and Ballard, two men held in the jail for the killing of Charley Martin.

That night the town was in great excitement, and the militia turned out and guarded the jail until about 3 a.m., when the crowds dispersed. The Times correspondent wrote that the town was 'filling up rapidly with excited men and neighbors of the girl to assist in the hanging,' who had come 'on a fruitless errand.'

The grand jury at Bellefontaine indicted Whitmore for murder in the first degree for poisoning his wife, and indicted Albert Hoge for shooting Charles Martin. No report of a trial or of any action against the crowd appears in the coverage.

Most papers treated the case as a crime story, and wire briefs carried from Delaware to Tennessee told of the poisoning and the dying statement without mentioning a mob. The same paragraphs ran in papers in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Mississippi, Arkansas and Missouri during the first two weeks of October. The Chicago Daily Tribune headed its dispatch 'Murder or Suicide?', setting the wife's declaration against the husband's denial.

The threatened lynching reached print chiefly through the Times correspondent's dispatch, reprinted in the Ottawa Free Trader under 'Wife Murder in Ohio,' which called the death 'one of the most horrible affairs that has ever blackened the history of this country' and referred to Whitmore as 'the villain.' That account treated a hanging as a likely result of local anger and did not criticize the crowd. The Columbus Westbote headed its report 'Der Lynchjustiz entgangen' ('escaped lynch law') and named the sheriff. The Black-press collection does not reach back to 1881.

Accounts differ on the wife's age, given as 14 by the Times correspondent and the wire brief and as 16 by the Westbote, and on whether the children in the woods were her siblings or her brother's children. The Times dispatch, dated October 1, put the mob threat on 'tonight', while the Westbote dispatch of October 4 placed the crowds on the previous night, after the Monday examination.

accounts.gist: Sheriff Cline drove Whitmore away by wagon, also fearing for two other prisoners; militia guarded the jail until the crowds dispersed at 3 a.m.

framing.detail: The Times correspondent called the poisoning 'one of the most horrible affairs' and Whitmore 'the villain', and presented a lynching as a possible outcome, citing the 'Shell case', without comment on the mob.
Der Westbote headed its report 'Der Lynchjustiz entgangen' (escaped lynch law) and described the sheriff's removal as saving the prisoner.
Wire briefs in Tennessee and Delaware told the poisoning story only.
